When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'permanently humiliated' is hard to reconcile unless the illness involved a specifically shaming interpersonal circumstance; nothing else in the profile suggests that context. The other items center danger, fear, vivid reliving, and generalized threat, so humiliation stands out as clinically mismatched to the trauma type.

vignette:
Robert, a 78-year-old divorced database administrator, had always taken pride in his physical independence and mental sharpness. That changed abruptly eighteen months ago, when a crushing chest pain sent him to the emergency room. He was diagnosed with a severe myocardial infarction and spent ten days in the cardiac intensive care unit, including a night when his heart stopped and he was resuscitated. The memory of that night remains vivid: the antiseptic scent of the unit, the hum of the monitor, the cold plastic of the oxygen mask. When he recalls the event, he often feels the sensation of his chest tightening, and the smell of isopropyl alcohol-a faint trace that sometimes drifts from his own bathroom-can make him feel as if he is back in that bed, reliving the moment the defibrillator paddles were placed on his chest. The memory does not feel like a recollection; it feels more real than the present, as though the hospital room has swallowed his living room.

These intrusive sensory flashbacks have reshaped how Robert sees the world. After a particularly vivid olfactory recall that left him drenched in sweat and gasping for air, he came to the quiet, devastating conclusion that life itself had become a hostile landscape. He lost his faith in the idea that people or time could offer safety. His body, once a reliable vessel, now seemed like an enemy that had nearly killed him and could do so again without warning. The world, he now believes, is a treacherous place where threat lurks behind every ordinary moment. This conviction took root gradually, each reliving episode reinforcing the thought that nowhere is truly safe.

At home, Robert is constantly on guard. He checks his pulse several times an hour, and a sudden change in his heart rhythm-a skipped beat or a flutter-sends him into a spiral of fear and shame. He feels angry at his own body for betraying him, and he cannot shake the sense that danger is imminent even when he is sitting in his armchair. This hypervigilance, which he cannot turn off, deepens his belief that the world is dangerous: if he must be this watchful inside his own locked apartment, then surely the outside world is worse. He has stopped going to the grocery store, relying instead on delivery, and he avoids phone calls with his daughter because her concerned voice makes him feel exposed and vulnerable. At work, where he manages databases remotely, the sound of a new email notification-unexpected, sudden-makes him jump, and he often logs off early, convincing himself that the stress of the job is a trigger for another heart attack.

The cycle tightens. A flashback leads to a new appraisal of danger, which heightens his hypervigilance, which then confirms that the world is indeed unsafe. He has become a prisoner of his own apartment, his own body. The negative emotions-fear, anger, shame-are almost constant. He no longer calls his former colleagues; he has let his friendships wither. He spends most of his time sitting in a recliner, monitoring his chest, waiting for the next smell or sensation to pull him back to that ICU bed.

What finally brought Robert to seek help was a panic attack three weeks ago, triggered by the smell of bleach from a cleaning wipe he used on his keyboard. He called his daughter, terrified, and she drove him to a clinic. Now, sitting in the therapist's office, he admits he is afraid of everything-the future, his heart, a stray scent on the air. But he is also, quietly, hoping that someone can help him untangle the knot of memory and dread that has tightened around his life.
